# USPS

A reusable .NET 10 library for validating and standardizing US addresses with the
[USPS Addresses 3.0 API](https://developers.usps.com/addressesv3).

*This library was generated by Claude (Anthropic) from the official USPS OpenAPI specifications;
review it before depending on it.*

Give it an address; it gives you back one of four things:

| Outcome | How you get it |
| --- | --- |
| A validated address, with anything USPS corrected or completed (ZIP+4, abbreviations, casing) | `AddressValidationResult` with `Status == Validated` |
| USPS could not validate the address | `AddressValidationResult` with a failure status and populated `Errors` |
| Anything else USPS reports — several matches, a building found but a unit number missing, delivery-point metadata | `AddressValidationResult` with `MultipleMatches` / `DefaultAddress`, plus `Corrections`, `Matches`, `Warnings`, `AdditionalInfo` |
| The request itself failed — unreachable service, missing API key, bad credentials, throttling, server fault | an exception derived from `UspsException` |

The distinction is deliberate: *"this address does not exist"* is an answer, so it is a result.
*"I could not ask"* is a failure, so it throws.

---

## Layout

```
USPS.slnx
src/USPS.AddressValidation/    the library (the published NuGet package)
tests/USPS.Tests/              unit tests (mocked HTTP) + live integration tests
samples/USPS.SampleApp/        runnable console demo
.github/workflows/ci.yml       build, test, pack, publish
```

---

## Getting credentials

The library uses the current USPS APIs at `apis.usps.com`, which authenticate with OAuth 2.0
client credentials — not the retired Web Tools `USERID`.

1. Sign in to the [USPS Business Customer Gateway](https://cop.usps.com) and go to
   **My Account → API Licenses → Add an Addresses API License**.
2. On the [USPS Developer Portal](https://developers.usps.com), add an app and copy its
   **Consumer Key** and **Consumer Secret**.

Those two values are `UspsOptions.ClientId` and `UspsOptions.ClientSecret`.

---

## Quick start

### Without a container

```csharp
using USPS.AddressValidation;
using USPS.AddressValidation.Models;

var validator = UspsAddressValidator.Create(new UspsOptions
{
    ClientId = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("USPS_CLIENT_ID"),
    ClientSecret = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("USPS_CLIENT_SECRET"),
});

var result = await validator.ValidateAsync(
    AddressInput.Create("3120 M St NW", city: "Washington", state: "DC"));

if (result.IsValid)
{
    Console.WriteLine(result.Address);            // 3120 M ST NW, WASHINGTON DC 20007-3704
    Console.WriteLine(result.Address!.FullZipCode); // 20007-3704

    foreach (var change in result.Changes)
        Console.WriteLine(change);                // ZipCode: (empty) -> '20007'
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{result.Status}: {result.ErrorMessage}");
}
```

### With dependency injection

```csharp
services.AddUspsAddressValidation(configuration.GetSection(UspsOptions.SectionName));

// or
services.AddUspsAddressValidation(options =>
{
    options.ClientId = "…";
    options.ClientSecret = "…";
    options.Environment = UspsEnvironment.Production;
});
```

`IUspsAddressValidator` and `IUspsTokenProvider` are registered as singletons so the OAuth token is
cached across calls, while each request draws a pooled `HttpClient` from `IHttpClientFactory` so
handler rotation keeps working.

Configuration binds from the `Usps` section:

```json
{
  "Usps": {
    "ClientId": "your-consumer-key",
    "ClientSecret": "your-consumer-secret",
    "Environment": "Production",
    "Timeout": "00:00:30"
  }
}
```

| Option | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ClientId` / `ClientSecret` | — | Consumer Key and Consumer Secret. Required. |
| `Environment` | `Production` | `Production` (`apis.usps.com`) or `Testing` (`apis-tem.usps.com`). |
| `BaseAddress` | — | Overrides the endpoint entirely. Useful for a proxy or a test double. |
| `Scope` | `addresses` | OAuth scope requested with the token. |
| `Timeout` | 30s | Per-request timeout. |
| `TokenExpiryBuffer` | 60s | Renew the token this long before USPS says it expires. |
| `UserId` | — | Value for the `X-User-Id` header, if your USPS account needs it. |

---

## Reading a result

```csharp
var result = await validator.ValidateAsync(input);

switch (result.Status)
{
    case AddressValidationStatus.Validated:
        // Exactly one delivery point. result.Address is the standardized form.
        break;

    case AddressValidationStatus.DefaultAddress:
        // The building exists but needs an apartment/suite/box number.
        // result.Address still holds the standardized default address.
        break;

    case AddressValidationStatus.MultipleMatches:
        // Several addresses match; ask the user for more detail.
        break;

    case AddressValidationStatus.InvalidInput:
        // Rejected by this library before any call was made. result.Errors names the fields.
        break;

    default:
        // AddressNotFound, InvalidAddress, InvalidCity, InvalidState, InvalidCityState,
        // InvalidZipCode, InsufficientInput, Unknown — USPS could not validate it.
        break;
}
```

Useful members:

- `IsValid` — `true` only for `Validated`.
- `Address` — the standardized `UspsAddress`; `ToAddressLines()` renders it as mail-piece lines.
- `Changes` — every field USPS `Completed` or `Corrected`, so you can show the user a diff.
- `Corrections`, `Matches` — USPS code/text pairs (`31` exact match, `32` default, `22` multiple).
- `Warnings` — free-text warnings from USPS.
- `AdditionalInfo` — delivery-point metadata: `DpvConfirmation`, `CarrierRoute`, `CountyName`,
  `IsBusiness`, `IsVacant` and, in `Extensions`, every other field USPS returned.
- `Errors` — why it failed, each tagged `Local` or `Usps`.

### Local checks

Before spending a call, the library validates the input against the constraints in the USPS
specification: a street address is required; either city **and** state, or a ZIP Code; the state
must be one of the 62 codes USPS accepts; ZIP Codes must be five digits and ZIP+4 four. Failures
come back as `Status == InvalidInput` with the offending field named — no request is sent.

---

## Exceptions

All derive from `UspsException`.

| Exception | When |
| --- | --- |
| `UspsConfigurationException` | Missing Consumer Key or Secret, or an unusable endpoint/timeout. Thrown when the client is constructed. |
| `UspsAuthenticationException` | USPS refused the credentials, or answered `401`/`403` after a token refresh. |
| `UspsRateLimitException` | `429`. Carries `RetryAfter` when USPS supplied the header. |
| `UspsApiException` | Any other unexpected status code, such as `500`. Carries `StatusCode`, `ErrorCode`, `ResponseBody`. |
| `UspsTransportException` | The service could not be reached: DNS, TLS, connection refused, timeout. |
| `UspsSerializationException` | USPS answered `200` with a body that does not match the documented shape. |

A `401` on the Addresses API is retried once with a fresh token before it throws.

## Running the sample

```bash
dotnet user-secrets set "Usps:ClientId" "<consumer key>" --project samples/USPS.SampleApp
dotnet user-secrets set "Usps:ClientSecret" "<consumer secret>" --project samples/USPS.SampleApp
dotnet run --project samples/USPS.SampleApp
```

It walks through nine addresses covering an exact match, a completed ZIP+4, standardization, a
default match, addresses USPS rejects, and input rejected locally — then deliberately points at an
unreachable host to show the exception path.

Validate one address instead:

```bash
dotnet run --project samples/USPS.SampleApp -- --street "3120 M St NW" --city Washington --state DC
```

Credentials can also come from environment variables (`Usps__ClientId`, `Usps__ClientSecret`) or
command-line switches (`--Usps:ClientId`, `--Usps:ClientSecret`).

---

## Running the tests

```bash
dotnet test
```

The unit tests drive the client through every USPS response shape with a stubbed
`HttpMessageHandler`, so they need no network and no credentials.

The integration tests hit the real API. They **skip** unless credentials are configured, so
`dotnet test` stays green without them:

```bash
dotnet user-secrets set "Usps:ClientId" "<consumer key>" --project tests/USPS.Tests
dotnet user-secrets set "Usps:ClientSecret" "<consumer secret>" --project tests/USPS.Tests
dotnet test
```

Or with environment variables — `USPS_CLIENT_ID`, `USPS_CLIENT_SECRET`, and optionally
`USPS_ENVIRONMENT=Testing`.

Run only the live tests:

```bash
dotnet test --filter-trait "Category=Integration"
```

The repository's `global.json` opts `dotnet test` into the Microsoft Testing Platform runner, which
xunit.v3 requires on the .NET 10 SDK.

## Releasing to nuget.org

[`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](.github/workflows/ci.yml) builds and tests every push to `main` and
every pull request. Pushing a version tag additionally packs and publishes:

```bash
git tag v1.2.3
git push origin v1.2.3
```

The tag is the single source of truth for the version — `<Version>` in the csproj is only a local
default and never needs editing to cut a release. A tag that is not a valid semantic version fails
the build before anything reaches nuget.org. Prerelease tags work too: `v1.3.0-beta.1`.

### Authentication: Trusted Publishing, not an API key

Publishing uses [Trusted Publishing](https://learn.microsoft.com/nuget/nuget-org/trusted-publishing).
The workflow asks GitHub for a short-lived OIDC token, nuget.org validates it against a policy you
register once, and hands back an API key that is valid for **one hour** and tied to that single
run. Nothing long-lived is stored in the repository.

This is now the only practical option as well as the recommended one: nuget.org caps newly created
API keys at 30 days, so the old approach means rotating a secret every month.

**One-time setup on nuget.org** — sign in, click your username, choose **Trusted Publishing**, and
add a policy:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Repository Owner | the GitHub user or organisation that owns this repository |
| Repository | this repository's name |
| Workflow File | `ci.yml` — **file name only**, no `.github/workflows/` prefix |
| Environment | leave empty, unless you uncomment `environment: nuget` in the publish job, in which case it must match exactly |
| Scopes | **Push new packages and package versions** |
| Glob Pattern | `USPS.AddressValidation` |
| Packages | leave unticked — the list only offers packages that already exist |

Three things that trip up a first release:

- **The scope must allow new packages, and the glob is the only way to name one.** The *Packages*
  checkbox list contains only packages that already exist under your account, so
  `USPS.AddressValidation` will not be there before the first release. A glob pattern, by contrast,
  also applies to packages matching it that do not exist yet — which is what authorises the very
  first push. Pair it with the *Push new packages and package versions* scope; the
  new-versions-only scope rejects a first release.
  A pattern with no wildcard matches that one id exactly, which is the tightest useful scope. Use
  `USPS.AddressValidation*` instead if you expect sibling packages such as
  `USPS.AddressValidation.Abstractions` later — note there is no dot before the `*`, or the main
  package stops matching. Avoid `*`: it would let this one repository publish anything you own.
  The glob controls what *you* may push; it does not reserve the id against other users. That is
  [ID prefix reservation](https://learn.microsoft.com/nuget/nuget-org/id-prefix-reservation),
  a separate request.
- **Tighten the policy after the first release.** Once the package exists it appears in the
  *Packages* list. Selecting it there and narrowing the scope to new versions only means a
  compromised workflow can no longer create new package ids under your account.
- **The workflow file name is part of the policy.** Renaming `ci.yml` later silently breaks
  publishing until you update the policy to match.
- **On a private repository the policy starts "pending".** nuget.org keeps it active for 7 days
  while it waits for a first successful publish to learn the GitHub repository and owner IDs. Miss
  the window and the policy goes inactive — you can restart the 7 days at any time.

**Repository secret**

| Secret | Where | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NUGET_USER` | Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions | Your nuget.org username — the profile name, **not** your email address. It is an account name rather than a credential, but nuget.org recommends storing it as a secret; a repository variable works equally well if you prefer. |

Two optional secrets, `USPS_CLIENT_ID` and `USPS_CLIENT_SECRET`, let CI run the live USPS tests as
well. They are referenced in a commented-out block on the workflow's `Test` step; uncomment it and
add the secrets to enable them. Left off by default, a USPS outage or rate limit cannot fail a
release.

**How the job is wired**

```yaml
permissions:
  id-token: write          # lets the job request the GitHub OIDC token

- uses: NuGet/login@v1     # swaps that token for a 1-hour nuget.org key
  id: login
  with:
    user: ${{ secrets.NUGET_USER }}

- run: dotnet nuget push "artifacts/*.nupkg" --api-key "$NUGET_API_KEY" ...
  env:
    NUGET_API_KEY: ${{ steps.login.outputs.NUGET_API_KEY }}
```

`id-token: write` is granted on the publish job alone, and the key is exchanged in the step
immediately before the push, so it cannot expire while the build is still running.

### Before the first publish

- **Claim the package id.** `USPS.AddressValidation` was unregistered on nuget.org at the time of
  writing, but ids are first-come. Publishing the first version claims it.
- **Set the repository URLs.** `RepositoryUrl` and `PackageProjectUrl` in the csproj are
  `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO` placeholders. The workflow overrides both from the Actions
  context, so packages built by CI are always correct; fix them anyway so local `dotnet pack`
  produces the same thing.
- **Check the author and copyright.** `Authors`, `Company` and `Copyright` are all `CDB`, and the
  `LICENSE` file names the same copyright holder.
- **Consider gating the publish.** The `publish` job has a commented-out `environment: nuget`.
  Create that environment and add required reviewers to make every release a manual approval —
  then set the same environment name on the trusted publishing policy.

### What the package contains

Packed from `src/USPS.AddressValidation`, with `lib/net10.0`, XML documentation for IntelliSense,
the MIT licence, this README as the listing page, and a `.snupkg` symbol package pushed alongside.
SourceLink (built into the .NET SDK) stamps the commit into the package, so consumers can step into
the source from a debugger — which is why the workflow checks out with full history rather than a
shallow clone.
